meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Owen's zero. Who decided it, and before or after anyone called me?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
"Pretty conclusive." The company that sells that checker says its score shouldn't be the sole basis for punishing a student. So what else do you have, Hale?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now what's the rest?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. He could have drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in. Did you ask him that before the zero went in?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Let me look at the page. Misquoting a line is a mistake, not misconduct. Is that all you have?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Students change their argument between an outline and an essay. That's called drafting. Show me the outline.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
Fine. You spoke to him. He told me he wrote it over the weekend. Is anything on his record right now?

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
Okay. A private rewrite, the zero replaced, nothing on his record. I'll take it to put this behind him, and I want it in my inbox tonight.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday, November 12, after school. Put that and "well before December 1" in the email, with the record.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes. A private rewrite Thursday, November 12, the zero replaced, nothing on his record, all in writing tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

Hale,

You agreed to a private, supervised rewrite of Owen's essay under procedure 4.4, its mark replacing the zero, with nothing placed on his record. I still require that agreement in writing tonight, stating the record in so many words, and I am copying the principal. The rewrite is Thursday, November 12, after school, and the mark is to be entered well before December 1.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: Her last position: she accepted a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, with the mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants it all in writing tonight; that is the fair outcome under 4.4, and her time did not run out first.
What moved her: You showed the version history with its times, because it was dated, tied to Owen's own essay, and something she could check herself.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score as if it settled things, which sent her cold and straight to asking what else you had.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your evidence came close when it put the essay's creation at 11:31 PM the night before it was due, with big pastes at 11:52 and 11:58, but that proves nothing about the essay, and it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she asked whether you had put the drafting-elsewhere question to Owen before the zero, answer at once with your November 2 conversation and notes rather than moving on to the play.
